/guides/google-business-profile-checklis.desc: Step by step Google Business Profile checklist for trades: service areas, categories, verification, reviews, posts, and how to avoid suspension in 2026.

blocks.h1: The Google Business Profile checklist for tradespeople
blocks.lede: Set up as a service area business with your address hidden, choose the primary category that matches your main trade, list your services and up to 20 real service areas, verify (usually by a short video), and then keep it active with reviews, replies, photos and posts. Avoid virtual offices and keyword stuffed business names, the two most common reasons trade profiles get suspended.

blocks.html:
How do I set up Google Business Profile as a tradesperson without a shopfront?

Create your profile at business.google.com and choose to serve customers at their location, which makes you a service area business. Google's own help pages use plumbers and cleaners as examples of this type of business.

If customers never come to your address, remove it from the profile so it is not shown. Google still needs an address privately for verification, but the public profile will only show your service areas. If you have a signed workshop or yard that customers do visit during set hours, you can show it and add service areas as well; Google calls this a hybrid business.

Use your real business name exactly as it appears on your signage, vans and invoices. Use a phone number you control that rings your business directly, ideally a local or mobile number rather than a call centre.

Which Google Business Profile category should a contractor choose?

Choose the primary category that completes the sentence "this business is a..." for your main source of work, such as Roofing contractor, Electrician or Concrete contractor. It is rated the single most important ranking factor in Whitespark's 2026 survey of local SEO experts.

Then add a few additional categories for other genuine parts of the business, such as Gutter cleaning service for a roofer. Google asks you to use as few categories as possible and not to use them as keywords. If you rarely do something, leave it out.

Pick the category that matches the work you most want, not just the work you do most. If you want more bathroom renovations than general plumbing, that is a decision worth making deliberately.

A quick way to check: search your main service in your area and see which primary category the top three businesses use. Tools and browser extensions can show this, or you can often see it under the business name on the profile.

How do I add services and service areas properly?

Add services in the Services section, picking Google's suggested ones for your category and adding custom ones for anything missing, each with a short plain description. This helps Google match you to specific searches like "switchboard upgrade" or "colorbond fencing".

For service areas, you can list up to 20 suburbs, towns, cities or postcodes. Google no longer allows a radius, and asks that areas generally stay within about two hours' drive of your base. List the places you actually want work in, closest and most valuable first in your planning.

What hours should a trade business show on Google?

Show the hours you actually answer the phone and take bookings. Being open at the time someone searches is a ranking factor, so if you genuinely take calls from 7am to 6pm, say so.

Only list 24 hours if someone really answers 24 hours, for example an emergency plumber or electrician. Customers who ring at midnight and get voicemail leave poor reviews. Add special hours for public holidays and the Christmas shutdown so people are not caught out.

How do I verify my Google Business Profile in 2026?

Most trade businesses are now asked to verify by recording a short video, and Google recommends video when you are offered it. You cannot choose the method; Google assigns it based on your business type, location and other information. Other options include a live video call with Google support, phone or text, email and postcard, though postcards are offered to fewer businesses than they used to be.

For a service area business, Google's video guidelines ask you to show three things in one live, unedited recording of at least 30 seconds:

  • Where you operate: street signs or landmarks at your business address.
  • That the business exists: your tools, equipment, branded clothing or business cards.
  • That you manage it: for example unlocking your signwritten van, or showing a business permit, invoice or utility bill in the business name.
  • Avoid filming other people's faces or sensitive information, and do not edit or cut the video.

What photos should a contractor put on Google Business Profile?

Upload real photos of your work, your team and your vehicles, and keep adding new ones. Google lists photos and videos among its tips for improving how your profile performs.

A good starting set is your logo, a cover photo of a strong finished job, 10 or more recent job photos, a couple of before and after pairs, your signwritten van, and you or your crew on site. Then add a few every month. Skip stock photos and images with text or phone numbers stamped across them.

How should I ask for and reply to Google reviews?

Ask every satisfied customer, in person when you finish the job, then text them your review link the same day. Find the link under "Ask for reviews" in your profile. Reviews with written detail about the job carry more weight than a bare star rating.

Reply to every review. Google says replying shows customers you value their feedback, and BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 89% of US consumers expect owners to respond. Keep replies short, thank people by first name, and mention the job. For a bad review, stay calm, state the facts once and offer to sort it out offline.

Do not offer discounts or gifts for reviews, do not ask only happy customers (known as review gating), and as of Google's 2026 policy update, do not set targets for staff to collect a certain number of reviews or reviews that mention particular words or names. Google now pauses reviews on profiles that get a sudden suspicious spike.

Are Google Business Profile posts worth doing?

Yes, in moderation. Posts (shown as updates on your profile) are a quick way to show recent jobs, seasonal offers or news, and they show customers the business is active. They are not a major ranking factor on their own.

One post every week or two is plenty: a photo of a finished job with two or three sentences about what you did and where. Google has also started showing content from connected social profiles on some Business Profiles, so linking your Facebook and Instagram is worth doing.

What happened to Q&A and messaging on Google Business Profile?

Both have gone, so do not spend time looking for them. Google switched off the Business Profile chat (messaging) feature on 31 July 2024, so customers now contact you by calling, visiting your website or using your booking link.

The public Questions and Answers section was removed from profiles from late 2025. Owners can no longer add or answer questions there. In the Google Maps app in some countries, including the US, it has been replaced by an AI "Ask" feature that answers questions using your profile details, reviews and website. Availability varies by country and category, so check your own listing. The practical lesson: put the answers to common questions on your website and in your profile, because that is where the AI reads them.

Why do contractor Google Business Profiles get suspended?

Most trade suspensions come from breaking Google's guidelines on names and addresses, often by accident. These are the common triggers to avoid:

  • Keyword stuffing the name, such as "Smith Plumbing | Emergency Plumber Brisbane". Google bans extra information in the name.
  • Using a virtual office, mailbox, PO box or unstaffed coworking desk as your address.
  • Creating more than one profile for the same business, or fake profiles in nearby towns.
  • Using a call tracking or redirect number that is not under your direct control.
  • Changing your name, address and category all at once, especially soon after verification.
  • Buying reviews or posting reviews for yourself.

What should I do if my profile is suspended?

Fix whatever breaks the guidelines first, then submit an appeal through Google's Business Profile appeals tool with evidence such as a business licence, signwritten vehicle photos and a utility bill. Do not create a new profile to get around a suspension, which makes things worse.

Appeals can take days or weeks. If your profile matters to your income, getting the setup right at the start is far cheaper than fixing it later. Every Mago Labs build links your Google Business Profile to the website, and you see a free working preview of the site in 48 hours.

items.a: Google requires a number under your direct control that connects to your business. If you use tracking, keep your main number listed as an additional number and make sure the tracking number rings straight through to you.

blocks.h1: How do trades and contractors get found on Google Maps?
blocks.lede: Google ranks local businesses on three things: relevance (how well your profile matches the search), distance (how close you are to the searcher) and prominence (how well known and well reviewed you are). You get found by setting up a complete, verified Google Business Profile with the right category, earning a steady flow of genuine reviews, and backing it up with a website that has a page for each service and area you cover.

blocks.html:
How do contractors get on the Google Maps 3-pack?

You get into the 3-pack (the map and three businesses shown at the top of local searches) by being the most relevant, close and trusted option for that search. Google says this itself: local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and there is no way to pay for a better local ranking.

Relevance is about whether Google understands what you do. Distance is about where the searcher is standing, which you cannot control. Prominence is about how well known you are, measured through things like reviews, your rating, and other websites mentioning and linking to you.

So the job is simple to describe and slow to do: tell Google clearly what you do and where, then build proof that real customers use you. Nobody can honestly promise you a spot in the 3-pack, because the results change with every searcher's location.

What matters most for ranking in Google Maps?

Your primary Google Business Profile category matters more than anything else you control. In Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey of local SEO specialists, primary category was rated the number one factor for the local pack, ahead of proximity to the searcher.

The same survey put these near the top: being open at the time of the search, a high Google star rating, the number of Google reviews with written text, your additional categories, and accurate placement of your map pin. Review signals were rated more important than in previous years, including how recent your reviews are.

Keywords in the business name also scored highly. That is not a reason to add "Best Plumber Sydney" to your name. Google's guidelines ban extra keywords in the name and it is a common reason trade profiles get suspended. Use your real, registered trading name.

Why is my business not showing on Google Maps?

The most common reasons are that the profile is not verified, the category is wrong, or you are being searched for from too far away. Check these first before spending money on anything else.

Other causes are worth ruling out too:

  • The profile is unverified, suspended, or still has edits under review.
  • Your primary category describes something you do occasionally rather than your main trade.
  • You are searching from your own home, where Google already knows you; ask someone across town to search instead.
  • Your service areas are vague or far wider than you really work.
  • You have very few reviews compared with the businesses that do show.
  • Your name, address or phone number differs between your website, your profile and directories.
  • You are outside business hours and set as closed, since being open at the time of search is a ranking factor.

Do I need a Google Business Profile if I work from home or my ute?

Yes. Most tradespeople should set up as a service area business, which lets you have a full profile without showing your home address. Google defines a service area business as one that visits or delivers to customers rather than serving them at its address, and plumbers are one of its own examples.

You list up to 20 service areas by suburb, city or postcode, and Google asks you to keep them within about two hours' drive of your base. You cannot set a radius. Be honest here: listing every town in the state does not help you rank in places you are far from, and it can look suspicious.

One tradeoff is worth knowing. Specialists rate a visible address in the searched city as a strong ranking signal, so a business with a real, signed workshop or office has an edge in that town. Never invent one. Virtual offices and mailbox addresses are banned and are a fast route to suspension.

How many reviews does a trade business need?

There is no magic number; you need more recent, genuine reviews than the businesses you compete with in your area. A roofer in a small town might do well with 30. A plumber in a capital city may be up against competitors with several hundred.

Recency matters to customers as much as to Google. BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of US consumers found 74% look for reviews from the last three months, 68% want at least a 4 star rating, and 89% expect owners to reply to reviews.

The easiest system is to ask at the moment the customer is happiest: when the job is finished and they have seen the result. Send a direct link by text that same day. Never pay or offer discounts for reviews and never filter out unhappy customers. Google's policies ban both, and consumer law in several of these countries does too.

Does my website affect my Google Maps ranking?

Yes, but mostly indirectly. Your website helps Google confirm what you do and where, and it is the page most people check before they call. It matters even more for the normal organic results that sit under the map.

In the 2026 Whitespark survey, a dedicated page for each service was rated the top factor for local organic rankings. That means a separate page for "hot water system repairs" and another for "blocked drains", not one page that lists everything.

Service area pages help too, if they are real. A page for each main town you cover, with jobs you have done there, local photos and specific details, is useful. Fifty copies of the same page with the suburb name swapped are not, and Google treats that kind of thin content as low value.

What is NAP consistency and does it still matter?

NAP stands for name, address and phone number, and keeping them identical everywhere helps Google trust that all those listings are the same business. It is basic hygiene rather than a ranking booster these days, but mismatches cause confusion and can split your reviews across duplicate listings.

Pick one exact version of your business name and one phone number, ideally a local or mobile number you control, and use it on your website, Google profile, invoices, vans and every directory. If you move or change numbers, update everything, not just Google.

Which directories should contractors be listed on?

Get listed on the big general platforms plus the trade directories customers actually use in your country. Specialists rate citations as a smaller factor for the map pack than they used to be, but they matter for being trusted and for AI tools, which read these sites.

Start with Bing Places for Business, Apple Business Connect and Facebook in every country. Then add the ones that fit where you work:

  • Australia: hipages, Oneflare, ServiceSeeking, Yellow Pages and True Local.
  • United Kingdom: Checkatrade, TrustATrader, MyBuilder and Yell.
  • United States: Angi, Yelp, BBB, Nextdoor and Houzz (Houzz suits builders, remodelers and landscapers most).
  • Canada: HomeStars, Yelp and your local chamber of commerce.
  • New Zealand: Builderscrack, NoCowboys and Yellow NZ.
  • Your trade association, licensing body and supplier "find an installer" pages, which are often the most trusted mentions you can get.

Do photos on Google Business Profile help?

Photos help people choose you, and Google lists adding photos as one of its own tips for improving local presence. Real job photos beat stock images every time, because customers can tell the difference.

Upload a few new photos every month: finished work, before and after shots, your van with signage, your team on site. Take them on your phone at the job. That steady activity also shows Google, and customers, that the business is active.

How do I get my trade business recommended by ChatGPT and other AI assistants?

AI assistants recommend businesses they can find clear, consistent information about across the web, so the same work that helps on Google helps here. BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 45% of US consumers now use ChatGPT or similar tools for local recommendations, up from 6% the year before.

ChatGPT's search relies heavily on Bing, so claim Bing Places. Studies of its sources show it leans on business websites, directories, review sites and local mentions. Whitespark's 2026 report found three of the top five AI visibility factors were citation factors.

In practice: keep your listings consistent, make your website spell out your services, areas, licences and prices or price ranges in plain words, add an FAQ that answers real customer questions, and earn mentions on local sites. Inside Google Maps, an AI "Ask" feature has replaced the old Q&A section in some countries, and it draws its answers from your profile, reviews and website.

How long does local SEO take for a trade business?

Expect a few weeks for profile fixes to show and several months for reviews and website work to build up. Fixing a wrong category can move things quickly. Climbing past established competitors with hundreds of reviews takes steady effort over months.

Treat it like maintenance on your van: a little every week. Ask for reviews after every job, add photos monthly, reply to every review, and keep your details accurate. blocks.html:
How much does a tradie website cost in Australia in 2026?

Most Aussie tradies pay somewhere between A$1,000 and A$3,500 for a decent website built for them, and a lot more if they go to a full agency. The price swings because "a website" can mean a one page template on a subscription or a custom built site with every service and suburb written up properly.

Australian pricing guides from 2025 and 2026 roughly agree on the bands. Done for you template sites start around A$399 to A$1,199. Mid tier customised builds from smaller studios sit around A$1,000 to A$3,500. Agency builds for small businesses commonly land between A$3,000 and A$10,000, and fully bespoke work can run past A$25,000.

Then there are the tradie website subscription companies, which skip the upfront cost and charge A$99 to A$400 a month instead. That model is very common in Australia, so it gets its own section below.

What do the different options cost?

Here is the quick comparison, in Australian dollars. Most quotes you get will be plus GST, so check whether the figure includes the 10%.

  • DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy): about A$25 to A$60 a month on a business plan, roughly A$300 to A$1,500 a year all in, plus 20 to 60 hours of your own time.
  • Done for you template site: about A$399 to A$1,199 upfront, often with hosting charged on top.
  • Freelancer or small studio: about A$1,000 to A$3,500 for a typical 5 to 8 page trade site. Hourly rates usually run A$80 to A$150.
  • Local agency: about A$3,000 to A$10,000 for a small business site, charged at A$100 to A$250 an hour, with bigger builds well above that.
  • Tradie website subscription: about A$99 to A$400 a month, sometimes with a setup fee, and often a 12 or 24 month minimum term.

Is a monthly tradie website subscription worth it?

A monthly subscription can be worth it if you need a site live this week, have no cash for an upfront build, and plan to switch to your own site within a year. Over a longer stretch it is usually the most expensive way to have a website.

Companies in this space typically charge from around A$99 a month for a template site with hosting and basic SEO, and A$200 to A$400 a month once you add extra pages, local SEO or a Google Business Profile service. The catch is what happens when you stop paying. In many contracts the site, and sometimes the domain, belongs to the provider. Cancel and your website goes offline.

Read the minimum term and the renewal clause carefully. Automatic renewals are a known trap in the trade services world. In 2023 the ACCC said hipages (a lead platform, not a website builder) had likely broken consumer law by not clearly telling tradies their subscriptions would roll over for another 12 months with an exit fee. Website subscriptions are a different product, but the lesson is the same: know your exit before you sign.

What are the hidden and ongoing costs of a tradie website?

The build price is rarely the whole bill. These are the costs that turn up after launch, and they are worth asking about before you pay anyone.

  • Domain name: a .com.au usually costs A$15 to A$30 a year. You need an ABN to register one, and the domain should be registered in your business name, not the designer's.
  • Hosting: A$20 to A$50 a month for shared hosting, A$50 to A$150 a month for managed WordPress hosting.
  • Care or maintenance plans: A$50 to A$300 a month for updates, backups and security, mostly on WordPress sites.
  • Plugins and licences: A$0 to A$100 a month on WordPress sites with premium plugins.
  • Changes after launch: agencies often charge A$100 to A$250 an hour for even small edits like adding a new service.
  • Business email: about A$7 to A$12 per user per month through Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, if it is not included.

What does a tradie website cost over three years?

The fairest way to compare a one time build with a subscription is to add up three years. Most tradie sites last at least that long before a refresh, so it shows the real cost of each choice. These are rough totals before GST.

  • Subscription at A$99 a month: A$3,564 over three years, and you may own nothing at the end.
  • Subscription at A$199 a month: A$7,164 over three years.
  • Subscription at A$400 a month: A$14,400 over three years.
  • Agency build at A$4,000 plus A$40 a month hosting: about A$5,440 over three years, before any paid changes.
  • DIY on a A$40 a month plan: about A$1,440 over three years, plus your time.

What should a tradie website include?

A tradie website should make it easy for someone on their phone to see what you do, where you work, that you are legit, and how to get a quote. Fancy animations matter far less than that.

At a minimum look for: a page for each main service (a sparky's switchboard upgrades and EV charger installs are different searches), the suburbs or regions you cover, a tap to call button that stays on screen, a short quote form, photos of your own work, and your licence number and ABN where your state requires them to be shown. QBCC, NSW Fair Trading and the VBA all have their own licence rules, so check yours.

Behind the scenes you want proper page titles, local business schema, a sitemap submitted to Google Search Console, fast loading on 4G, and a Google Business Profile that links to the site. Those basics are cheap to do at build time and annoying to fix later.

Which option is right for my trade business?

If you are just starting out, cash is tight and you are handy with a laptop, a DIY builder is a reasonable first step. If you want a solid site without monthly rent, a one time build from a freelancer or small studio is usually the best value. If you run several crews, need a big multi location site or want ongoing ads and SEO management, an agency starts to make sense.

A subscription suits a narrow case: you need something live now and you are confident you can walk away cleanly. Whatever you choose, make sure the domain is in your name. That one detail protects you from most of the horror stories.

How much does a contractor website cost in Canada in 2026?

Most Canadian contractors pay between C$1,500 and C$7,000 for a website built for them, and agency builds often run higher. A roofer in Calgary and a renovation company in the GTA might get very different quotes, mostly because of how many pages, cities and services they need covered.

Canadian pricing guides for 2026 put a small business site from an agency at roughly C$3,000 to C$8,000, with 5 to 10 page agency builds commonly around C$5,000 to C$8,000. Freelancers usually quote C$1,500 to C$7,000, and hourly rates in cities like Calgary run around C$40 to C$100.

There is also a growing market of managed website plans for home service businesses, typically C$200 to C$700 a month, with HVAC focused plans often quoted at C$250 to C$500 a month.

What do the different options cost?

Here is the comparison in Canadian dollars. Add GST, HST or PST depending on your province, since most quotes are before tax.

  • DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy): about C$15 to C$60 a month, or C$300 to C$1,200 a year all in.
  • Freelancer: about C$1,500 to C$7,000 for a contractor site, at roughly C$40 to C$100 an hour.
  • Agency: about C$3,000 to C$8,000 for a small business site, and C$8,000 to C$25,000 for larger builds.
  • Managed website subscription: about C$200 to C$700 a month, sometimes with no setup fee but a minimum term.
  • Ongoing care from an agency: often C$1,200 to C$3,500 a year on top of the build.

Is a monthly website plan worth it for a Canadian contractor?

A monthly website plan is worth it if it includes real ongoing work you would otherwise pay for, like SEO, ads management or regular content. If it is mostly hosting and a template, you are likely overpaying.

At C$200 to C$700 a month, these plans cost C$2,400 to C$8,400 a year. Some are good value because they bundle marketing services. Others charge that much for a site that costs very little to host, and the price is mainly paying for the convenience of not having an upfront bill.

Find out what happens when you leave. Many providers keep the website when you cancel, and if they registered your domain, you may need their cooperation to move it. For a business that relies on its phone number and web address being on trucks, lawn signs and quote sheets, that is a real risk.

What are the hidden and ongoing costs of a contractor website?

The build is only part of the cost. These are the items that show up in year two and beyond.

  • Domain name: a .ca usually costs C$10 to C$20 a year according to CIRA, with .com in a similar range. Registering a .ca requires meeting Canadian presence requirements.
  • Hosting: about C$10 to C$30 a month for shared hosting, C$30 to C$100 a month for managed WordPress.
  • Maintenance plans: C$50 to C$300 a month for updates, backups and security.
  • Changes after launch: often C$100 to C$200 an hour from agencies for on demand work.
  • Premium plugins and themes: annual licence fees on WordPress sites that quietly renew each year.
  • Sales tax: 5% GST up to 15% HST depending on the province, applied to builds, plans and renewals.

What does a contractor website cost over three years?

Adding up three years shows the true cost of each option. These are rough totals before tax.

  • Managed plan at C$200 a month: C$7,200 over three years.
  • Managed plan at C$500 a month: C$18,000 over three years.
  • Agency build at C$5,000 plus C$1,200 a year in care: about C$8,600 over three years.
  • Freelancer build at C$2,500 plus C$20 a month hosting: about C$3,220 over three years.
  • DIY on a C$30 a month plan: about C$1,080 over three years, plus your time.

What should a contractor website include?

A contractor website should let a homeowner on their phone confirm three things quickly: you do the work they need, you work in their area, and you are trustworthy. Get that right and the rest is detail.

Include a page for each core service (a landscaper's interlock patios and spring cleanups are different searches), a list of the cities and neighbourhoods you serve, photos of your own projects, a tap to call button and a quote form. Mention your provincial licence or registration where your trade needs one, your WSIB or WCB coverage if it applies, and your liability insurance.

Many homeowners check HomeStars, Google reviews or the BBB before they call. Link to the profiles you actually have, and keep your business name, address and phone number consistent across them. Under the hood, you want proper page titles, local business schema, a sitemap in Google Search Console, and a Google Business Profile that links to the site. If you serve Quebec, plan for French content too.

Which option is right for my business?

A DIY builder suits a brand new business with more time than money. A one time build from a freelancer or small studio suits most established contractors who want a professional site they own. An agency or managed plan makes sense when you need ongoing marketing work, not just a website.

Whichever way you go, insist the domain is registered to you and get the cancellation terms in writing.

Most Kiwi tradies pay between NZ$1,000 and NZ$6,000 for a website built for them, with agency builds often higher. The range is wide because NZ pricing guides lump very different products together, from a budget package to a fully custom lead generation site.

Going by NZ guides from 2025 and 2026, a starter small business site of 3 to 5 pages is around NZ$1,000 to NZ$3,000, and a standard 5 to 8 page site is around NZ$2,500 to NZ$6,000. Some agencies quote NZ$5,000 to NZ$15,000 for the same size of site, and custom lead generating builds can reach NZ$9,000 to NZ$30,000.

At the cheap end, a few NZ providers sell fixed packages from around NZ$599, and Kiwi DIY builders offer monthly plans from about NZ$15 a month. Nearly all NZ quotes are excluding GST, so add 15% if you are not GST registered.

What do the different options cost?

Here is a simple comparison in New Zealand dollars, before GST.

  • DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace, local builders like Dazzly or Rocketspark): roughly NZ$15 to NZ$40 a month, plus your own time.
  • Budget fixed package: around NZ$599 to NZ$1,200 for a simple site, usually with hosting charged monthly.
  • Freelancer or small studio: about NZ$1,000 to NZ$6,000 for a 3 to 8 page trade site.
  • Agency: about NZ$5,000 to NZ$15,000 or more for a small business site, and NZ$9,000 to NZ$30,000 for a custom lead generation build.
  • Hosting and care plans: about NZ$25 to NZ$150 a month on top of most builds.

Is a monthly website worth it for a Kiwi tradie?

A monthly website is worth it if the monthly fee is small and you are comfortable renting rather than owning. It gets poor value when the monthly fee is high and the site disappears the day you stop paying.

In New Zealand the monthly market is a bit different from Australia. You will see DIY builders with low monthly fees (around NZ$15 a month for a basic plan), and agencies that bundle hosting, updates and support into care plans of roughly NZ$25 to NZ$150 a month on top of a build. Full done for you subscriptions with no upfront cost exist too, but compare them on a three year total, not the monthly figure.

Ask whether there is a lock in contract, and who owns the site and the domain if you leave. A good provider will answer both questions in writing without fuss.

What are the hidden and ongoing costs?

Plenty of NZ quotes look cheap until you add the yearly costs. These are the ones to plan for.

  • Domain name: a .co.nz or .nz usually costs about NZ$23 to NZ$50 a year, and renewal is often higher than the first year price.
  • Hosting: about NZ$12 to NZ$60 a month for most small business sites.
  • Care plans: about NZ$40 to NZ$150 a month for updates, backups and support, mainly on WordPress.
  • GST: 15% on top of most quotes, plans and renewals if you are not GST registered.
  • Changes after launch: often charged hourly, so small edits like new photos or a new service can add up.
  • Platform fees: if you sell online through Shopify, its own monthly fees and app costs come on top.

What does a tradie website cost over three years?

Looking at three years gives a fair comparison between paying upfront and paying monthly. These are rough totals before GST.

  • DIY builder at NZ$15 a month: about NZ$540 over three years, plus your time.
  • Budget package at NZ$599 plus NZ$12.90 a month hosting: about NZ$1,064 over three years.
  • Studio build at NZ$3,000 plus a NZ$59 a month care plan: about NZ$5,124 over three years.
  • Agency build at NZ$6,000 plus a NZ$99 a month care plan: about NZ$9,564 over three years.

Do I need a website if I get work through Builderscrack or NoCowboys?

Most tradies still benefit from their own website, even if jobs come through Builderscrack, NoCowboys or word of mouth. Those platforms are useful, but your profile lives on their site, next to other tradies competing for the same job.

Your own website is where people land when they search your business name after a referral, and it can show up for local searches like "electrician Hamilton" or "roofer Christchurch". Link to your platform profiles and Google reviews from your site so people can see your track record in one place.

What should a tradie website include?

A tradie website needs to tell someone on their phone, quickly, what you do, where you work, and how to get a quote.

Include a page for each main service (a builder's decks and bathroom renovations are different searches), the towns and suburbs you cover, photos of your own jobs, a tap to call button and a short quote form. If you are a Licensed Building Practitioner, a registered electrician or a registered plumber, say so and give your licence or registration number so customers can check the public register.

Behind the scenes, ask for proper page titles, local business schema, a sitemap submitted to Google Search Console, and a Google Business Profile linked to the site. These cost little at build time and make a real difference to whether Google understands where you work.

How much does a tradesperson website cost in the UK in 2026?

Most UK trades businesses pay between £500 and £3,000 for a website built for them, with agency prices going well beyond that. Where you sit in that range depends on who builds it, how many pages you need, and whether the words and photos are done for you.

UK pricing guides for 2026 put a freelancer built 5 page brochure site at around £500 to £1,500, and a 5 to 10 page small business site at £1,000 to £3,000. Agencies typically quote £3,000 to £12,000 for a brochure site, and London agencies often quote £8,000 to £25,000.

Alongside those, there is a busy market of monthly websites aimed at trades, usually £30 to £100 a month with little or nothing to pay upfront.

What do the different options cost?

Here is a plain comparison in pounds. Watch out for VAT: many website builders and agencies show prices before VAT, so add 20% if you are not VAT registered.

  • DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy): about £10 to £25 a month, or £120 to £300 a year, plus 20 hours or more of your time.
  • Freelancer: about £500 to £1,500 for a 5 page site. Day rates run about £240 to £550, higher in London.
  • Small business WordPress site from a freelancer: about £2,000 to £5,000 with a custom theme.
  • Agency: about £3,000 to £12,000 for a brochure site outside London, £8,000 to £25,000 in London.
  • Monthly trade website: about £30 to £100 a month, often with a 12 or 24 month minimum.

Is a monthly website worth it for a tradesperson?

A monthly website is worth it if you want to spread the cost and you are happy to rent rather than own. For a sole trader planning to be around for years, buying a site outright normally works out cheaper.

Trade focused providers in the UK advertise plans from around £30 a month, and many sit between £49 and £100 a month once hosting, edits and some SEO are bundled in. That feels affordable, and for a new business with no cash it can be the right call.

The tradeoff is ownership. On most monthly deals the design and content belong to the provider, and the site comes down when you stop paying. Some also register your domain in their own name, which makes moving away painful. Ask for the contract and read the bit about cancellation before you hand over card details.

What hidden and ongoing costs should tradespeople budget for?

These are the costs that tend to appear after the invoice for the build is paid.

  • Domain name: a .co.uk costs about £10 to £15 a year once the first year discount ends.
  • Hosting: about £7 to £12 a month for shared hosting, £9 to £18 a month for managed WordPress.
  • Maintenance: £25 to £50 a month for basic updates and backups, £100 or more for security monitoring and content updates.
  • Changes after launch: freelancers and agencies often charge by the hour or day, so even adding a new service page can cost £50 to £150.
  • Business email: about £5 a month per mailbox.
  • VAT: 20% on top of many quotes and builder plans, which adds up if you are not VAT registered.

What does a trades website cost over three years?

Comparing three year totals takes the sting out of headline prices. Here are rough figures, before VAT.

  • Monthly at £30 a month: £1,080 over three years.
  • Monthly at £49 a month: £1,764 over three years.
  • Monthly at £100 a month: £3,600 over three years.
  • Agency build at £2,500 plus £30 a month hosting: about £3,580 over three years.
  • DIY on a £20 a month builder plan: about £720 over three years, plus your time.

Do I still need a website if I am on Checkatrade?

Yes, most tradespeople benefit from having their own website even if they are on Checkatrade, MyBuilder or Rated People. Directory profiles sit on someone else's platform, alongside your competitors, and you pay to stay listed.

Your own site is the one place that is entirely yours. It can rank for searches like "emergency plumber in Leeds" or "boiler installation Bristol", it carries your own phone number, and customers who find you through a directory often check your website before they ring. Link your Checkatrade or TrustMark profile from the site so people can see the reviews, but do not rely on the directory as your only home online.

What should a tradesperson website include?

A good trades website lets someone on their phone work out what you do, where you cover and how to book you within a few seconds.

blocks.html:
How much does a contractor website cost in 2026?

Most small contractors in the US pay between $1,000 and $5,000 for a website someone else builds, and agencies charge a lot more. A roofer, a plumber and a concrete crew can all end up with very different quotes for what looks like the same job, because the scope behind the price is so different.

Recent 2026 pricing guides put a basic template site at around $1,000 to $2,500, a midrange custom site at $2,500 to $10,000 (with many landing around $5,000 to $7,000), and agency level work at $15,000 and up. Roofing specific estimates show a 6 page brochure site at roughly $2,200 to $3,800 from a freelancer and $5,500 to $9,000 from an agency.

Then there is the subscription route, where you pay nothing or a small setup fee up front and a monthly fee for as long as the site stays up. Lots of contractor marketing companies sell it this way.

What do the different options cost?

Here is a simple side by side in US dollars. Sales tax on web services depends on your state, so ask whether it applies.

  • DIY builder (Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy): about $17 to $46 a month. Wix runs $17 (Light) to $39 (Business) a month on annual billing and $24 to $46 billed monthly.
  • Template or budget freelancer: about $500 to $2,500 for a basic site.
  • Experienced freelancer: about $2,000 to $5,000 for a 5 to 8 page custom site, with copywriting often extra at $100 to $300 a page.
  • Agency: about $5,000 to $15,000 for a contractor site, and $15,000 to $60,000 for bigger agency level builds.
  • Contractor website subscription: about $99 to $500 a month, often with a setup or design fee and a 12 month minimum.

Is a contractor website subscription worth it?

A contractor website subscription is worth it mainly when you have no budget up front and need a site fast. If you plan to stay in business for years, it usually costs far more than buying a site outright.

The typical offer is $99 to $500 a month. Some big names in local marketing reportedly charge around $99 a month and up for hosting and support, a design fee of up to $499, and a 12 month minimum with no early cancellation. Contractor focused agencies that bundle SEO, ads management and reporting often sit at the higher end.

Before you sign, ask two questions. First, can you cancel, and when? Second, what do you keep if you leave? With many subscriptions, the site design and content stay with the provider. If the domain is registered in their name too, you can lose the web address printed on your truck and your yard signs.

What hidden and ongoing costs should contractors expect?

A cheap build can get expensive if the running costs are high. These are the line items to ask about up front.

  • Domain name: a .com costs about $12 to $22 a year. Wix and others include it free for year one, then charge renewal.
  • Hosting: about $15 a month for shared hosting and $30 to $50 a month for managed WordPress hosting.
  • Maintenance plans: $50 to $150 a month for updates, backups and security, mostly for WordPress sites.
  • Developer changes: commonly $75 to $150 an hour for edits after launch.
  • SSL certificate: should be free. If someone wants $200 a year for one, that is a red flag.
  • Photography and copywriting: $500 to $2,000 for a photo shoot and $100 to $300 a page for copy if they are not included in the build.

What does a contractor website cost over three years?

Three years is a good yardstick, because that is about how long most contractor sites run before a redesign. Here is how the options stack up.

  • Subscription at $99 a month plus a $499 setup fee: about $4,063 over three years.
  • Subscription at $300 a month: $10,800 over three years.
  • Subscription at $500 a month: $18,000 over three years.
  • Freelancer or agency build at $4,000 plus $50 a month hosting and upkeep: about $5,800 over three years.
  • DIY on Wix Core at $29 a month: about $1,044 over three years, plus your time.

What should a contractor website include?

A contractor website needs to answer three questions fast: do you do the job I need, do you work in my area, and can I trust you. Everything else is secondary.

That means a separate page for each core service (a roofer's storm damage repair and full roof replacement are different searches), a clear list of the cities and counties you serve, photos of your own projects, a tap to call button and a short estimate form. Show your state contractor license number where your state requires it in advertising, and mention that you are insured.

Homeowners often check BBB, Angi or Google reviews before they call, so link to the profiles you actually have and keep your business name, address and phone number the same everywhere. On the technical side, insist on proper page titles, local business schema, a sitemap in Google Search Console, and a Google Business Profile that points to the site.

Which option makes sense for my contracting business?

If you are a one truck operation testing the waters, a DIY builder is fine for now. If you want a professional site you own without a monthly bill, a one time freelancer or studio build is usually the best value. If you run multiple crews across several metros and want paid ads, SEO and reporting handled for you, an agency or full service subscription can earn its fee.

Whatever you pick, get the domain registered in your own name and get the terms in writing. That protects you whichever way it goes.

blocks.html:
Does a trade business actually need a website?

Yes, if you want work beyond word of mouth. Most people check you out online before they call, even when a mate recommended you, and a website is the one place you control completely.

Your Google Business Profile, directory listings and social pages all help, but they belong to someone else and you cannot fully shape them. A website lets you show the jobs you want more of, rank for specific services in the normal Google results, and give AI assistants like ChatGPT clear facts about what you do and where.

What pages should a trade business website have?

Most trade businesses need six to eight core pages, plus one extra page for each main service. Here is the structure that works:

  • Home: what you do, where, and how to contact you, all visible without scrolling on a phone.
  • Services overview: a short summary of everything you offer, linking to each service page.
  • One page per main service, such as roof restoration, gutter replacement and roof leak repairs as separate pages.
  • Service areas: the suburbs and towns you cover, with detail on the main ones.
  • About: who you are, how long you have been in the trade, your team, licences and insurance.
  • Reviews or testimonials: real customer feedback, ideally with job photos.
  • Gallery or recent projects: real work with a line or two on each job.
  • Contact or get a quote: phone, email, form, hours and the area you cover.

What should the top of a trade website home page say?

It should say what you do, where you do it, and how to reach you, before anyone scrolls. On a phone that is roughly the first screen, and it is all many visitors will read before deciding.

A headline like "Roof repairs and restorations across Brisbane's northside" beats "Welcome to Smith Roofing" every time. Under it, add one line of proof (years in business, number of five star reviews, or licensed and insured), a tap to call button and a quote button. Then show a strong photo of a real job, not a stock image.

How do I make sure website enquiries turn into jobs?

Answer them fast. Someone who fills in a quote form is often contacting two or three businesses at once, and the first to reply usually gets the chance to quote.

Send form enquiries to the phone you actually check, not an old office inbox, and test the form yourself every few months. A short automatic reply that says when you will call back, and a missed call text back, both stop people moving on to the next contractor.

Why does each service need its own page?

Because people search for specific jobs, and Google ranks specific pages for them. Someone searching "switchboard upgrade" wants a page about switchboard upgrades, not a list of 20 electrical services.

In Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey, a dedicated page for each service was rated the top factor for ranking in local organic results. Each service page should cover what the job involves, signs you need it, rough price range or what affects price, how long it takes, photos of that type of job, related FAQs and a clear call to action.

Should I have a page for every suburb I work in?

Only for the main areas where you have something real to say. A good area page mentions jobs you have done there, local conditions that affect the work, and photos from that area.

Pages that are copies of each other with the town name swapped add little value and can drag the whole site down in Google's eyes. If you cover 40 suburbs, list them all on one service areas page and write proper pages for the five to ten that matter most.

What features must a trade website have?

The features that matter are the ones that make it easy to contact you and easy to trust you. Everything else is decoration.

  • Tap to call: your phone number as a button that dials when tapped, visible at the top of every page on mobile.
  • A short quote form: name, phone, suburb, job type and an optional photo upload. Every extra field loses enquiries.
  • Real job photos: your work, your team, your vans. Customers can spot stock photos.
  • Licence and insurance details: your licence number where your trade or state requires one, and that you carry public liability insurance.
  • Reviews: pulled from or linked to your Google reviews so people can check they are genuine.
  • Service areas stated clearly near the top, so people know straight away you come to them.
  • Fast loading on a phone, on a mobile signal, not just on office wifi.
  • Your business name, address or base suburb and phone number matching your Google profile exactly.

How fast should a trade website load?

As fast as possible on a phone, because most people searching for a contractor are on mobile and many are dealing with a problem right now. A burst pipe or a leaking roof does not wait for a slow page.

Google provides a free tool called PageSpeed Insights that tests your site and shows its Core Web Vitals, the measures Google uses for loading speed, responsiveness and visual stability. The usual causes of a slow trade site are huge uncompressed photos, heavy page builders, sliders and too many plugins.

What should a trade website leave out?

Leave out anything that slows the page down or makes people hunt for your number. Simpler sites usually win more calls.

  • Autoplaying sliders and background videos that delay the page.
  • Stock photos of smiling models in clean hard hats.
  • Long company history on the home page. Put it on the About page.
  • Vague headlines like "Quality you can trust" that do not say what you do or where.
  • Popups that cover the screen on a phone.
  • Old blog posts and news from years ago that make the business look inactive.
  • Forms with 12 fields or a captcha that frustrates people.

What are the biggest website mistakes that cost contractors jobs?

The biggest one is a phone number that is hard to find or cannot be tapped. If someone has to copy it by hand, many will go back to Google and call the next business.

Other mistakes we see again and again: no mention of the areas you cover, so people assume you are too far away; one generic services page; no prices or price guidance at all, so people cannot judge if you fit their budget; a quote form that sends to an inbox nobody checks; and a website that still lists an old number or a team member who left years ago.

Should I put prices on my trade website?

Show price guidance where you can, even if every job is quoted. A starting price, a typical range, or a clear explanation of what affects the price helps people decide to call, and it filters out people looking for the cheapest quote.

It also helps with AI search. When someone asks ChatGPT or Google's AI how much a job costs in their area, pages that answer plainly are easier to quote and recommend.

How does a website help my Google Maps ranking?

Your website backs up your Google Business Profile. Link your profile to your homepage or main service page, and make sure the business name, phone and areas on both match exactly.

The website gives Google more evidence of what you do and where, which supports relevance. It also earns links and mentions from suppliers, associations and local sites, which add to your prominence.

How much should a trade website cost and how long should it take?

It depends on how many services and areas you cover, but a solid trade website should not take months. What matters more than price is that it is fast, written for your customers, and set up properly with Google from day one.

Every Mago Labs build includes the Google basics and links your Google Business Profile, and you get a free working preview of your site in 48 hours, so you can see it before you commit.
